description:
This is a review of the EVGA RTX 3060 XC Blaaand it's gone. It's all gone. The RTX 3060 XC Black benchmark tests gaming performance vs. RTX 3060 Ti, 2060, 960, & more.
Sponsor: ASUS TUF Gaming B550 Plus WiFi on Amazon - https://geni.us/DbWZ

Our stuff is ACTUALLY in stock: Grab a GN Toolkit on the store for GPU tear-down & maintenance (in stock & shipping now, including signed versions) https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/gamersnexus-tear-down-toolkit
Grab a GN Wireframe Mouse Mat for a desk-sized, high-quality mousing surface (in stock & shipping now): https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/gn-wireframe-mouse-mat

Watch our RTX 3060 XC Black tear-down & disassembly: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJFJ_clQT8U

The NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU comes out today, and we're reviewing it with the EVGA RTX 3060 XC Black. Testing includes basically every modern card, but we primarily compare the RTX 3060 vs. the RTX 3060 Ti, RX 6800 & 5700 XT, RTX 2060, RTX 2060 Super, GTX 960, and GTX 1080 / 10-series cards. The RTX 3060 is a little bit disillusioning to review, if we're honest, and that's because we're all well aware at this point of the impossibility of meeting demand with any silicon product at launch. This isn't just NVIDIA: It's everyone, and not even just other PC part makers. Regardless, we'll review it from two perspectives: In the first, we're talking about today, and that means keeping perspective of availability and pricing. In the second, we're talking about the future -- hopefully helping someone at a time when cards are more readily available. Benchmarks for the RTX 3060 include power consumption, gaming (e.g. Cyberpunk 2077), thermals, and fan speed, alongside RTX game benchmarks for ray tracing.

Watch our GPU Testing Methodology (2020) here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-P7-ML-bPCE
Watch our GTX 960 4GB & 2GB revisit here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rPRqlg6l1ls

comments.text:
Considering the cut-down nature of the entire 4xxx lineup (basically shifted each one down one card title, 4060 is actually a 4050, ect) this is very true. If you can acquire a 12gb 3060 you will see some games easily using more than 8gb of Vram at 1080p, with higher settings. Where people might object to 3060 vs say a ti variant or 3070, is when you want higher settings at higher resolutions. 1440p is doable on this card. The tradeoff becomes FPS vs Resolution vs Settings. If you want high FPS and Resolution, gonna have to sacrifice settings. If you want high settings and FPS, gonna have to sacrifice resolution. If you want High resolution and high settings, gonna sacrifice FPS. 

For me, I can run Doom Eternal on 1080p with ultra settings, RTX/DLSS disabled, ~144 fps with this card. Vram usage creeps slightly above 10gb, with no noticeable frame dips or other issues. 

Similarly, Apex Legends will run at 144hz with maxxed settings. 

BF5 and GTA5 run between 60-100 fps. This card is pretty beast for the power draw, footprint, heat, ect. I went from a 980 to 3060. A 1080ti is roughly equivalent to the 3060.

comments.text: I wouldn't say that AMD/ATI's increase in the amount of VRAM and the potentially corresponding memory interface is mere "market," implying that they just threw it in the 6800 XT for bragging rights of people with too much money and insufficient understanding of contemporary hardware demands. Historically, ATI has been known, in general, for image clarity, stable/smooth framerates, and support for higher resolutions than nVidia's equivalent competition -- all of which are greatly affected by the amount of VRAM and memory interface! Furthermore, if we narrow the scope of this analysis down to the current competitive environment that AMD/ATI's 6000 line finds itself in, we see that AMD is still lagging behind in the realm of Ray Tracing and DLSS, which many people value for the FUTURE SOFTWARE ENVIRONMENT rather than the present. As we've seen, the average file size for games is going through the roof, and this is primarily due to higher resolution textures and higher polygon models; thus, because an increase in VRAM and memory interface is a TIME-TESTED method of increasing the effective lifespan of a video card, we can pretty safely assume that AMD did this as a reliable means of FUTUREPROOFING their card as best they could to make them more appealing & valuable to potential customers, given the shortcomings that they cannot snap their fingers to overcome.

comments.text:
​ @Zero-hw1il  First of all, under communism a government wouldn't exist because it's a theoretical form of anarchism. Now socialism on the other hand, saying that the government is able to "force more production of silicon" is great and all, but that's not how it works. Under a socialist system the economy is centrally planned. All prices, resource allocation and supply is controlled by the government. The item is literally going to have the price stamped on it. There is no need to force anything, the government controls the entire supply chain from raw resource to finished product to the actual store that sells the product AND they are also your employer which means they control your access to currency used to exchange for the product. Now, will you as the average person have any access to the product? That depends on where you live and other factors. The chance of the demand being lower than the supply for any even remotely desirable product is zero. So you will still be waiting in line to receive it or alternatively you'll be paying exorbitant prices on the black market in foreign currency. 
Will the government decide to produce more of the product if the demand is high? That also depends, if the product is necessary for worker productivity or compliance, there's a decent chance that production will be ramped up because the central planner is not oblivious to the product being useful. So something like food, alcohol, a tractor or other work vehicle for example, would be a high priority product. If it's a luxury product on the other hand, it's highly unlikely that supply would be ramped up unless resource availability and worker productivity reaches astronomical levels and supply of everything essential is far excess of demand. Keep in mind that in historic context, even food production has fallen short of demand a lot of the time. Humans aren't perfect nor is it easy to centrally plan an economy.

In capitalist systems based on supply and demand, things like food are massively overproduced because it's economically viable, which would be highly undesirable from a central planning perspective because it's a gross misallocation of resources.
comments.author: @tiikerihai
@tiikerihai

comments.text:
@Zero-hw1il  Are you stupid or simply not reading what I said? I explicitly stated that in a centrally planned economy prices are controlled by the state. There is no "unlikely to increase" involved here, prices would not increase or change at all unless the state was explicitly interested in lowering demand through price controls for whatever reason, yet most of the time that is unnecessary when it can simply create a shortage of supply while retaining existing price. The end result is the same. You cannot get the product because you're either A) priced out or B) have nowhere to get it from.  Eg you're dealing with a situation where demand is higher than supply not much different than what you get in a "free market" economy.
The reason I am ignoring your point of "these prices are directly caused by free market" is because A) I have not made a claim contrary which would require me to respond, B) this claim is oversimplified (we do not have a free market, market regulation exists and it does also affect prices as well as the ability to expand fabrication) so talking about it doesn't interest me C) I assumed you would be able to comprehend that it has nothing to do with what I'm saying or take issue with.

The idea that centrally planned economy is somehow more efficient producing anything is profoundly ignorant. The appeal of central planning isn't efficiency, it's control over direction. You have full control over the direction toward which resources are allocated whereas in a free market consumer demand dictates the direction and that isn't always for the betterment of society. To put it simple, in a free market economy resources are efficiently allocated toward whatever retarded pursuits the consumer demands while in a centrally planned economy resources are inefficiently allocated toward a concrete and "societally advantageous" pursuit.
The reason a centrally planned economy isn't efficient like a free market one, by the way, is because price in a free market is an automatic feedback loop that gives information to the suppliers on how much of a good they should produce through the demand in response to price. That does not exist in central planning.

comments.text:
That intro sums up the current GPU market fairly well.
I have myself long been thinking of going for a GPU upgrade myself, but with the current market it seems a bit lackluster to spend money on.
Though, I guess miners and scalpers will buy all the cards almost regardless of what the card is.

If I were nVidia or AMD I would look into leasing out the cards for a couple of months and have in the terms of service for the lease that mining isn't accepted. And that one can't resell the card. And only at the end of lease do the customer get to keep the card and do whatever they wish with it.

Then scalpers can't buy and resell the card. Since they only lease it and reselling it puts them in legal trouble where they can get fined.

Miners can't really get much use out of the card for the couple of months that it is leased. One can use some "always online DRM"-ish driver (here I would implement it so that it only occasionally needs to phone home, so just because you don't have internet for 3 days doesn't mean your card will lock up) for the lease period that checks for mining, if mining is detected, then the card shall be returned. (Here we would need to give some margin for false positives and occasional "mining" web pages and viruses...)

And people who buy the cards for productivity and/or gaming can use the cards like normal.

At the end of the maybe 3 month lease, the card is yours to keep. (and the "always online DRM"-ish feature turns off letting you use the card freely.)

Though, such a thing is really authoritarian and frankly not perfect. But at least it stops scalpers from being an extra price hiking middle hand in the market, and it stops the product from seeping into a segment that the card's aren't supposed to go to. All while ensuring that those that the product is marketed to gets to actually get the product. From a customer relations standpoint, it might be a net positive during times like these.
